d.title: The order a query is evaluated
d.caption: Written SELECT-first, executed FROM-first. Knowing the real order explains why a column alias from SELECT cannot be used in WHERE but can in ORDER BY, and why HAVING exists.

items.label: SELECT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT

d.title: The joins
d.caption: INNER keeps matches only; LEFT keeps every left row and fills the right with NULL; FULL keeps both sides. A LEFT join followed by WHERE right.col IS NULL is the anti-join: 'customers with no orders'.

columns.title: INNER
items: rows with a match on both sides

d.title: Normalise, then stop
d.caption: Split repeating groups into their own table (1NF), move columns that depend on part of a key (2NF), then columns that depend on other non-key columns (3NF). Beyond that, denormalise deliberately for read performance and say so.

nodes.label: 1NF
nodes.sub: atomic values, one row per fact

d.title: SQL injection, and the parameter that prevents it
d.caption: String formatting puts the user's text into the SQL; a parameter sends the SQL and the value separately, so the value can never be parsed as SQL. Every DB-API driver supports parameters; none require formatting.

d.title: Isolation levels and the anomalies they allow
d.caption: Higher isolation prevents more anomalies and costs more locking or retries. PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED; SERIALIZABLE may abort a transaction that must then be retried.

d.title: A database deadlock
d.caption: Transaction 1 updates row A then wants row B; transaction 2 updated B and wants A. The database detects the cycle, aborts one, and the application must retry. Updating rows in a consistent order prevents it.

d.title: SQLAlchemy's two layers
d.caption: Core builds and executes SQL as Python expressions over an engine and connection pool. The ORM sits on top, mapping classes to tables and tracking changes in a Session. You can use Core alone; the ORM always uses Core.

d.title: The unit of work
d.caption: Changes to mapped objects are recorded, not sent. flush() turns them into SQL in dependency order; commit() flushes and ends the transaction. Nothing reaches the database until one of those.

d.title: Reading an EXPLAIN plan
d.caption: Read from the innermost node outward: how each table is accessed, how the results are joined, then sorted or aggregated. A Seq Scan on a large table under a filter is the line that wants an index.

d.title: A zero-downtime column rename
d.caption: A rename in one migration breaks the running old code. Expand, migrate, contract: add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one — each step deployable on its own.

items.label: Deploy code that writes both
items.desc: reads still from the old column

items.label: Deploy code that reads the new column

d.title: Sizing a connection pool
d.caption: Every worker holds up to pool_size + max_overflow connections. Workers × pool must stay under the database's max_connections with room for migrations and admins — a limit hit at 3 a.m. by a scaled-up deployment.

d.title: Layering, with the dependencies pointing inward
d.caption: The domain knows nothing about the web or the database; the application layer orchestrates it; adapters translate to and from the outside world. Imports go downward only — an import from the API layer inside the domain is the smell to catch.

d.title: One artefact, many environments
d.caption: The same container image runs in dev, staging and production; only the configuration injected at start-up differs. Anything that differs by environment is configuration; anything that does not is code.

d.title: A trace is spans nested in time
d.caption: One request becomes a root span with child spans for each call it makes. The gaps and the longest child are where the time went; the trace id ties the spans together across services.

d.title: pre-commit, in the loop
d.caption: The hooks run on the staged files before the commit is created: format, lint, type-check. A failure stops the commit; the same hooks run in CI so nothing depends on every developer having installed them.

d.title: Docker layers, and what invalidates them
d.caption: Each instruction is a cached layer; a change invalidates it and everything after it. Copy the dependency manifest and install before copying the source, so a code change does not reinstall every package.

items.label: COPY . .   + CMD
items.sub: changes every commit — keep it last

items.label: RUN pip install / uv sync
items.sub: changes when the lock file changes

d.title: Build once, promote
d.caption: Tests run on the same artefact that ships. The image built on the commit is tagged, tested, then promoted to staging and production by tag — never rebuilt per environment.

d.title: Where a supply-chain attack gets in
d.caption: Typosquatted names, hijacked maintainer accounts, malicious install scripts and compromised build pipelines all deliver code through the same 'pip install'. Pinning with hashes, a private index and a lock file reviewed in code review narrow every entry.

d.title: Worker models
d.caption: Sync workers handle one request each; async workers handle many I/O-bound requests on one loop; a process per core gives the CPU parallelism the GIL denies threads. Gunicorn with uvicorn workers combines processes and async loops.

d.title: Mitigate first, then diagnose
d.caption: During an incident the order is fixed: stop the bleeding, then understand. Rolling back, scaling, or shedding load buys the time to look inside the process without users paying for it.

items.label: Mitigate
items.desc: roll back, restart, scale, feature-flag off

items.label: Preserve evidence
items.desc: logs, metrics, a py-spy dump or core before the restart

items.label: Diagnose
items.desc: correlate the change, the metric and the trace

items.label: Fix and verify
items.desc: a test that reproduces it, then the postmortem

d.title: Coupling, in concrete terms
d.caption: Coupling is how much of B you must know to change A. Low coupling is a narrow interface with data crossing it; high coupling is shared mutable state and reaching into internals.

d.title: Broadcasting stretches the smaller shape
d.caption: Shapes are compared from the right; a dimension of 1 is stretched to match. (3, 4) + (4,) works; (3, 4) + (3,) does not, because 4 and 3 disagree — reshape to (3, 1) first.
d.label: (3, 4) + (3,) → ValueError: operands could not be broadcast

d.title: Where SettingWithCopyWarning comes from
d.caption: df[df.x > 0] may be a copy or a view; assigning a column on it might modify a temporary that is thrown away. Use .loc[mask, 'col'] = value on the original, or .copy() explicitly when you mean a new frame.

nodes.label: df[df.x > 0]
nodes.sub: copy or view? pandas cannot promise

d.title: An idempotent pipeline step
d.caption: Running the step twice for the same partition gives the same result: it overwrites its output partition rather than appending. Retries and backfills become safe by construction.

d.title: The hidden-state problem
d.caption: Cells run in the order you clicked, not the order on the page. A notebook that passes 'Restart and run all' is reproducible; one that does not is a collection of results nobody can regenerate.

items.label: cell 1 uses df
items.desc: works — because of the order you ran them

items.label: Restart kernel, Run all
items.desc: the only test of a notebook

d.title: Leakage: fitting the scaler on all the data
d.caption: A scaler fit on train and test together has seen the test set's mean and variance. Fit every transformer on the training split only, inside a Pipeline, so cross-validation refits it per fold.

d.title: What a trained model actually is
d.caption: A model artefact is the learned parameters plus the code that interprets them plus the preprocessing that produced its inputs. Save and version all three together, or the loaded model silently disagrees with training.

d.title: Batching requests at inference
d.caption: Predicting one row at a time pays the fixed cost per call; collecting requests for a few milliseconds and predicting the batch amortises it. Latency rises slightly, throughput rises a lot.

d.title: Streaming tokens from an LLM API
d.caption: With stream=True the response arrives as server-sent events, one chunk of tokens at a time; the client yields them to the user as they come instead of waiting for the whole completion.

d.title: A semaphore bounds concurrency
d.caption: A thousand coroutines may exist, but only ten hold the semaphore at once; the rest wait. The API sees at most ten in-flight requests, which is the number you agreed to.

d.title: The sliding window
d.caption: Two indices bound a window that only moves forward. Extending the right edge adds an element; shrinking the left edge removes one; each element enters and leaves once, so the whole pass is O(n) instead of O(n²).
d.label: window [2, 5) sums to 10; slide right: add 9, drop 4

d.title: Trade memory for time
d.caption: The nested loop compares every pair — O(n²). One pass with a hash map remembers what has been seen — O(n) time, O(n) space. Nearly every 'find a pair' problem is this trade.

columns.title: two loops
items: for i: for j: if a[i]+a[j]==t

d.title: A min-heap is a complete tree in a list
d.caption: heapq keeps the list so that each parent is smaller than its children: the minimum is always at index 0. Push and pop are O(log n); the children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2.

d.title: BFS versus DFS
d.caption: Breadth-first uses a queue and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph; depth-first uses a stack (or recursion) and is the natural shape for exhaustive search and cycle detection. Both mark visited nodes to avoid loops.

d.title: Binary search halves the range
d.caption: lo and hi bound the candidates; mid is compared and half the range is discarded. log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 comparisons. bisect_left returns the insertion point, which is the idiom for 'first element ≥ x'.
d.label: target 12: mid=7 < 12 → search the right half; mid=12 → found at index 5

d.title: Backtracking explores and undoes
d.caption: Choose, recurse, un-choose. Each level of the tree is one decision; a branch that violates a constraint is pruned before it grows. The undo step is what makes the same partial state reusable across branches.
